correctness.rationale: The beta-integral gives marginal density 1/2, and converting to [0,1]^2 multiplies all energies by the same 2^(-beta). In the central square the log potential is continuous and has distributional Laplacian 2 pi f_3. If the potential were additive, the mixed derivative of its Laplacian would vanish; on the positive quadrant the mixed derivative of f_3 is strictly positive, as also witnessed by the strict rectangle difference in RESULT.md. Smoothing two pairs of coordinate point masses yields one fixed zero-marginal g with nonzero linear variation; the candidate densities are bounded below on its support uniformly near p=3. The densities converge almost everywhere and have mass one, so they also converge in L1. In passing to the limit in (r^beta-1)/beta the near-diagonal part is bounded by the locally integrable |log r| times a uniform local density bound; away from the diagonal the difference quotient converges uniformly. Thus the first and quadratic variations divided by beta have finite limits A_0 != 0 and B_0. Choosing one sufficiently small t of the sign of A_0 preserves feasibility and makes 2tA_0+t^2 B_0 positive for all sufficiently small beta. This proves the interval claim, not an explicit endpoint. The frozen checker was inspected, not executed; it only corroborates the rectangle sign, already proved by strict convexity.
